Thermal barrier coatings are being developed to protect air-cooled turbine blades and vanes in aircraft gas turbine engines.
The current state-of-the-art coating system consists of about 0.25 mm of a zirconia-yttria ceramic over 0.13 mm of an MCrAlY alloy bond coat, both applied by plasma spraying.
Coating failure is primarily due to stresses induced by the thermal expansion mismatch between the ceramic and metallic layers, influenced by oxidation and sintering.
The initial NASA laboratory model related coating life to the radial component of the thermal expansion mismatch strain (Cy) and the weight gain from oxidation.
The Pratt & Whitney model uses Miner's Law and calculates inelastic strain ranges from thermal expansion mismatch, heating/cooling transients, and elastic strain at yielding.
The Garrett model considers bond coat oxidation, zirconia toughness reduction, and damage from molten salt deposits, and includes empirical factors to match test data.
The General Electric model is the only one to consider failure induced by edges, including shear strain in the life correlation.
The Pratt & Whitney model is accurate to within a factor of 3 in predicting coating life across a wide range of test conditions.

Remaining uncertainties include the effects of creep and inelasticity, the detailed mechanisms of oxidation control, the importance of sintering and hot corrosion, and the validity of simplifying assumptions.
Future engine designs are expected to rely heavily on thermal barrier coatings, so accurate life models are required to assess risks and fully exploit the technology.
The NASA HOST program successfully integrated materials and structural aspects to produce design-capable thermal barrier coating life models.

Plasma-sprayed zirconia-yttria coatings exhibit very low thermal conductivity, high compressive strain tolerance, high in-plane tensile strain tolerance, creep-like behavior, and fatigue-like behavior.
The stress state in the ceramic coating layer is biaxial compression in the plane of the coating and radial tension, further complicated by a wavy interface.
Experimental evidence shows slow crack growth, creep, and fatigue-like behavior in plasma-sprayed zirconia-yttria coatings.
The design-capable models developed under the HOST program are now or will soon be used in the design of thermal barrier coatings for aircraft gas turbine engines.
